projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Kenneth Earl Hoffman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Kenneth Earl Hoffman. Mr. Hoffman served in the U.S. Army Air Corps with the 8th Air Force, 306th Bomb Group, 367th Squadron. He served in the European theater, and his highest rank was tech sergeant. I am Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Hoffman's home in Concord, Ohio, on February 22, 2005. Ken's wife was also present, and Ken was 81 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Lewisville, Ohio, born in Canton, Ohio. And, help me out here, keep going.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, when were you born?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: September 1st, 1923.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '23, so you were 18 when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and share your memories of that day.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Okay. I worked in the, my brother-in-law and sister's grocery store, and I don't know if I heard it over the radio, but I heard it, and I looked out the store window and I saw, some of the neighborhood guys got relieved at the time and I saw them walking back to the bus stop, so I knew, I knew then it was for sure. And, it was just, just about everything. I just kept working the grocery store for, and before that, after I got out of high school, I worked at a U.S. Navy ordnance at Bettis Westinghouse in Canton, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what your personal reaction was when you heard about the attack? How did you feel?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Well, I wasn't, I wasn't all that startled because I was up on the news, as I say, something is going to happen, and it was, it was a surprise shot, no doubt about it, and I didn't think, my first news, I didn't really think it would be that devastating, that they were, Japanese, how could they do something like that? Not that they could do it, the distance, I couldn't understand how they got the distance to do that much destruction. But, and I had, I had my military kind of lined up, for some reason, I just can't recall. I was 18 years old at that time. No, I was 19. So, I thought, well, they're going to hit me pretty good. So, a little bit ahead of the game, I went and enlisted in the United States Army Air Corps, and there was a reason I'm spelling it out now, but we'll get to it. And, so, I got kind of put on a hold, and then after I worked, I think six or eight months at Bettis Westinghouse, I got the time to call in, and it was, it was December 7, '43. Yeah, '43. Then, I went to Fort Hayes, Columbus, Ohio, and there was just a mess of guys down there, all over the place. In fact, this was Fort Hayes Army base, and they were so overflowing, they put us up in a hotel in downtown Columbus. First, we had to march back, but it wasn't that far. And then, we fooled around there and got our clothes and everything, and then, we got our orders to board a train, Miami Beach, Florida. My God, that's great, I'm going to Florida. I always wanted to go there, never got there. Got down there and they -- excuse me. Got the hiccups again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: You got to, got to Miami Beach off the train and it was cold, jeez, for down there. Hey, I thought it was supposed to be warm here. But anyhow, they put us in, all of us in, at that time, the new hotels. My God, I can't believe I got this, because I thought that was great. And then the Fonda Fiesta Hotel, I still remember the name. And I went through our basic training, marched to chow, marched back, and, I think, I think, anyways, from five to seven in each room, and cots we slept on. We started the basic training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day of basic training?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, yes, march, march, march, it was in step, 30-inch steps, 28-inch steps, something like that. We did that a lot at first. And then, of course, it was a physical, physical training for an hour each day, and then we got, then they started us on exams, put us in the category, what our capabilities were, and I fooled around with photography, I was a high school photographer, and went out for the interrogation. He's going to put me in the photographic section. I says, I want to be a gunner, I want to be an aerial gunner. So, he asked me questions of photography, and I, I purposely lied to him, gave him the wrong answers, and, oh, I guess you're going to be a gunner. He wanted me to go to the photographic section. So, from there, I liked it down there, it was, it was great. The food was good, really. We ate out of mess kits, we had to clean them each time we came to the mess hall, dunk them in scalding water, rinse them, then put them in rinse water again. And then we went through rifle training. I liked that. I did pretty good, really, and we still marched every day, even though we had to go to classes and that. Then, that was, jeez, I guess about three months, really. And I went through rifle drill, and I'm glad we did that, because I used that rifle drill all through VFW. I mean, I knew the port arms, I knew the side arms and I knew the whole show. I remember that. Then we went to, well, Texas. Amarillo, Texas. AM school. I thought that was good, because, and I didn't know anything about the school, but it was a complete airplane mechanics school. And I was, jeez, nine, ten months there. Got there, it was colder, you wouldn't believe, I was oh, my God, I'm going back to Florida. But, oh, going back to Miami, the only thing, we did get to walk on Collins Avenue a little bit, and I got my taste of coconut milk. I loved coconut, and they had the fruit stands all over the Collins Avenue. I'm going back to aviation school, each, I can't remember, each month or each week, we took one part of the airplane, and we went through everything, how it was put together, why it was put together, and, and I can't remember whether it was every week or every month. It might come to me. And, about everything, I mean, it was, I was not a scholar by a long spot, and I, I had a difficult time. I had really a difficult time, but I knew I had to learn, I was going to learn that stuff, and it didn't bother me that I was just going to be a gunner, but I wanted to know what the airplanes did, and that's a good thing because I needed that later on. Then, I was there eight or nine months. Then I signed up for gunner school. I went to Kingman, Arizona. That was great. I was firing .50 Caliber machine guns every day. And the last two, three weeks, we went to AT-6s, which is the open cockpit trainer plane, and we fired, fired area ground for awhile. And I saw the target but I saw the rabbit running over there, so I, instead of the target, I started shooting at the rabbit. Caught hell for that one. And then we went to air to air, through, the pilots were just going overseas, so they gave us an extra ride. We went through, we flew through the Grand Canyon, which to me was great, really. I got --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of plane were you flying through the Grand Canyon?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: AT-6s. It was great. Then, from there we went to Amarillo, Texas. I was in Texas a long time. And that was first phase training, where we got assigned to a crew and we started flying with the crew. We got to know each other, and our flight engineer got -- (Interview interrupted by coughing.) He got VD, so he busted from the crew and they put me in as flight engineer. I liked that because I was back in waist gunner, back there and shoot on the side, but then I got flight engineer, and I was helping out a lot. I mean, you know, check the instruments and, and some of the procedures, and I liked that. Then, the second month was final phase training. We went on bombing runs and we went, all the overseas training you needed. Then, that we went, Jesus, I don't know how I got so damn many places after that, building up to going overseas. So, after a few bases and, I learned more about the plane, it was B-17s, B-17s, and then we went to Presque, Maine. And we really got colder than hell again, always cold. Then, we got more cold air flight gear and the, the guard with the helmets and the whole business, and then the, they wouldn't let us fly the planes over there, they got the ferry group that, they flew it over, we just rode along, and we, we landed and, oh, we had snow for three months, snow, white, white, white, we dropped out of the skies, it was always cloudy over there, like it was here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So about when was it that you crossed?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: End of '40 -- end of '43.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: End of '43?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: I thought it was '42.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No, '42 was when I went in.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, because in '44 you were over there.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: I was over there November. Well, then we flew this crew, we flew to Presque, Maine. Then we were supposed to go to Labrador, but we had a tail wind, so they flew from Presque, Maine, to Nutscorner, Ireland. I'll never forget, Nutscorner, Ireland. Naturally, as a northern Ireland boy, I'm not going to make it here. Landed there, we're going to stay there overnight, we got bivouacked and, you're going to leave for England now. So, we got on a boat and went to England. This was a funny part, you know, it wasn't a troop ship, it was a, it wasn't a bus, it wasn't a, a GI truck or anything. We walked over this town, right on the border, I forget what it is now, it's right on the coastline. I don't know how we found our way, but we found another way. Then, we walked over the damn town trying to find the place we were supposed to get off, but we got there, and then we landed at, in England. Oh, a train took us, a train took us there, to England. How could I forget that town? In England.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: You'll think of it.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah. Anyhow, we got this thing, we got the base and we got climatized, so to speak, and we were supposed to go on our first combat mission, probably the last of '43 or the first of '44, and the pilot come down with a hernia operation, I guess. So, he was out of commission for two, three weeks. We just roamed around the base there, watched the combat crews come in and the combat crews go out. They'd send 25, 30 ships out and get five back. I says, I don't know if I made the right choice or not. Sometimes they sent 25 planes out, because that's, that's, that's all we could put out, but later on, we put 50 planes, squadron. There was four squadrons in a group, it was the 306th Group, Bomb Group, and the 367th Squadron. Each squadron would put out 50, 60 ships. And, so, we're getting ready to go, the pilot got out of the hospital and we're getting psyched up. So, we went on our first mission, Schweinfurt, Germany. I had read about Schweinfurt. I think, I don't know, we lost a hundred ships the first mission on Schweinfurt. I thought, oh, my God, I'll never make it, I'm not going to make it. And, of course, my -- okay, that first mission, they split the crew up. I went with an experienced crew. My radio operator, he got killed the first mission. We used to call him the man that came to breakfast. I know for sure I was not going to make Schweinfurt. So, we took off for Schweinfurt, and the old flak was so heavy that you could get out and walk on it. That was the terminology used in those days, and then we got over our target and dropped our bombs. Oh, God, we made it. And then I heard over the earphone, well, the lead ship didn't drop her bombs, we have to do a 360 and go over Schweinfurt again. Oh, God, we'll never make it the second time. So, well, long story short, we did. Made a lot of missions. First, when I first started, we only did 25, because a large percentage never made 25 missions. You either got shot down or you got killed. Then the, I'm getting close to 20, 21, my God, I may make it. Then, I got news, well, you're going to have to go to 30 missions. Oh, God, I'll never make it. So, I'm pumping 30, 31. No, I'm pumping 28, 29. I thought, hey, I may make it. So, then I got word, well, you've got to do 35 missions. I said, my God, somebody is after me. And, anyhow --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: When was D-Day in there?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, D-Day is December, or, no --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: I don't know which mission it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About which mission? That would be, you know, obviously June 6th of '44.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, June 6, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Six or seven months after you started flying, maybe?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, I had -- let's see, 25, 30. I had about 30 missions.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you fly missions on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. We were supposed to go twice but only went once. Cloud cover, always cloud cover. Sun don't shine in England, I guess. And I'm looking, I'm watching and I'm listening to the pilots, and we're about over Berlin, I looked down, I saw the, the stadium, and there was a break in the clouds, and I could see the stadium. My God, at least I get to see something. And Berlin was nothing, we didn't get any losses in Berlin. It was a, I won't say an easy target, but as far as losses, we didn't have. Berlin --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: How many planes were flying that day?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, on that day?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, my God.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: How many took off?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: I don't know. Hundreds. Hundreds. Four, five, maybe 600. B-17s, 24s, 25s, at the lower level. A lot of 25s didn't go the altitude, they stayed down the lower level, and wall-to-wall airplanes, bombers, as far as you could see all around you. I liked that because, hey, my odds jumped, went up a little bit, or down a little bit. Then --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, I'm guessing, you were in the 8th Air Force?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Which squadron?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Squadron?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bomb group?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: 306th. In fact, I've been looking, I get Air Force magazines, been looking for our group and squadron, and by God, we got one yesterday, I cut it out, with 306th and 367th. First thing I ever saw about them. All the other groups. We were triangle H, you can spot us on the tail as triangle H, triangle Cs, triangle H,

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: To reiterate a little bit, what I was telling you about, I watched in the training in Amarillo a fuel transfer, and I says, you know, I'm going to memorize this because I may need that because some things I look ahead on. And, oh, our 13th mission, we had a hell of a time there. We got knocked out of formation, we made a, we had a, I forget the target, but we went, we got number three engine shot out, and a piece of flak hit the oil rod and we lost oil. So, we had to shut the engine down because it's windmilling. And, so, the pilot calls me up, he says, I have to, we have to use, to get back, we have to use some of the gasoline out of number two engine since it was dead, and, and we need, we needed gas in number one engine. So, I says, okay, I'll take care of it, and I remembered. The pilot says, drain number two and put it in number one, and I says, Pete -- he was the pilot -- I says I can't do that. So, I had to go through, I had to transfer number two engine to number three tank and then take number three and, and, all I had to do was change tank valves and push the pump the right way, and he couldn't understand that right away. So, the reason I had to tell him was for the reason, I says, number one and two engine, which is lower on the gas, so I know which, which tank to put it in? So, he said two. So I put it in two, and I said, I'm going to put it in number one now, and watch your gauge, let me know, and we did it, we did it, we got back. That was just one of the many instances. One time, one time we, we lowered the bomb bay doors and dropped the bombs and we couldn't retract the bomb bay doors. So, I said, okay, I'll take care of it. I had to get out of the turret, go back to the bomb bay and get the hand crank. I'm on a six-foot walkway between, through the bomb bay doors there, you know, cranking, crank the bomb bay doors up, and I'm looking down at Germany down there. Oh, my God, I can't believe I'm doing this. So, did that, got through with it. That's, that's, that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have much fighter activity before D-Day? Did you have any encounters with German fighters?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Okay, let me re-track on that a little bit. At first when I started flying, after you hit the French coast, we had no bomber -- no fighter protection. They didn't have the range, the P-47s, so they turned around, and I knew they was coming up as soon as we hit that French coast, so I looked out there, and the Germans, 109s and Fokker 190s, waiting for us. That's another story. Be out there, and I was in the top turret on the front, so I just, that's why I liked it better, I was at the waist, I could see what in the hell was going on, and I'd see them lining up, they'd come in ten, 12, 13 abreast, just mow us down like, like cannon fodder. Sometimes, German fighter pilots were hotshots, man, we'd be within, I don't know, dozen feet or less formation, and they would barrel through, right through our formation, right in the middle of us. They were hotshots. They were hotshots. Of course, I fired at all of them, but I never, I never claimed a hit, because everybody was firing like, man, and who knows who what, hit what, but, and the planes, the bombers going down was -- let's see, what was it? I think it was at Schweinfurt. No, not the Schweinfurt. The one mission was terrible.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: I was just going to say something. Go ahead with what you were going to say.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: I looked back, that's another thing, boy, you turn that turret around, the view, and I looked back, as far as you could see, you could see fires where bombers went down, just a steady row of bombers that blew up and hit the ground.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Tell him about Dresden. Probably saw it in the paper about Dresden.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, yeah, my dad was held in a prison camp near Dresden, in fact.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, is that right?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Why you did Dresden.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Dresden was -- so you flew for about a year then, over there?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Almost.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, because when was Dresden, like February of '45?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: I wasn't in Dresden.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, I though you --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think that was like, it was in the paper because --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: It was later. It was later, '45.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: We just discussed Dresden.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah. The English wanted it. They've got to pay these guys back, I guess. I don't know why.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Well, the Germans had bombed all --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, the Germans bombed the hell out of a lot of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Coventry.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, that's right. And they leveled that poor town. They leveled it. There was nothing left of it. We went over there by the hundreds and chopped everything they had, which, war is war. Now, now they have that damned Senate investigation and everything else, and, God.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: They have wars, wars, wars.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other memorable missions?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, I could probably go on all night, but, oh, I still, I had my first five missions, waist gunner, and my other waist gunner got hit by flak, he got hit in the shoulder. I laid him down and looked at his wound, it was right in the shoulder. I went and got the morphine out. You're not going to -- he wouldn't have no part of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't want that?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No, but he was all right. He made it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Afraid he'd get addicted or something?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No, he was just afraid of me with a needle, I guess, more than getting shot.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: He didn't mind getting shot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any of your crew members during your tour? Other than, you told me about that first one.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: The radio operator. We lost the ball turret -- that's another story. As I say, I could go on all night with this stuff. Anyhow, the ball turret, he, I don't know, it was under five missions for the simple reason that I was still waist gunner. And, I don't know, one, two or three missions, he got out of his turret, he says I'm not getting back in the ball turret, and that was a, that was a vicious place. I crawled into the ball turret when we were still on the ground, and I was scared. That was a mean place. Anyhow, he crawled out and stood up in the middle of the plane the rest of the mission. So, about the fourth or fifth mission, he radioed he's coming out. I said no, you stay in there, just move your turret around, show that somebody is there. I'm coming out. So, I could still fire my waist gun and I put my foot on his door so he couldn't get out.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Nasty. I wouldn't put there in there. He might read it.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Well, he made it all right for the simple reason he quit. They made a CQ out of him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies on your crew?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Well, we all were close, all ten of us, but I had one buddy, he was in our outfit, so all through training and, I thought, oh, boy, be with us, and they put him in another group. That was a sad story, too. They got shot up, his crew got killed and he and somebody else, they were neither pilots, so the plane come back from England, they got to the air base, and he tried to land the plane, couldn't make it, he went around three times. Last time he cracked up and they all died. No, I was kind of a loner.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Well, you kept, you kept in touch with --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: -- the pilot.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: And the tail gunner.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: And the bombardier. The navigator. What was Gus?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Gus is the navigator. I don't know if he's still living or not. He was in pretty sad shape. Pete, the pilot, is dead. The tail gunner is in Texas. Florida.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Pete's in Texas.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No, I'm talking about Trigger, the tail gunner.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, he's in New Mexico.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: New Mexico, that's right. He's all right. He's good.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Trigger is all right.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: He's all right. He went on, he stayed in. And he's a good baseball player. Hell, he was operating on a baseball team somewhere. He got intelligence.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Tell him about Gus, when he got shot down.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, that's right. That's another story.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: This is funny. We need some hilarity.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: He was a tall, handsome.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, he was, yes. I met him, but he was...

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Okay, he, I don't know what happened, screwed up and took our navigator and took, took Gus out of our plane as a navigator and put him in another plane, and he flew off a right wing, and I got to watch, he got shot down. I saw him bail out, saw all of them bail out. In fact, the right wing got shot to hell and they started coming to us and, oh, my God, but anyhow, I didn't know until years later, I guess, what happened to him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Well, I don't think you ever saw him after that.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: You didn't know what happened.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No. But anyhow, he got shot down in Paris, and he landed --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: In France.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: In France, and they had this villa over there, and he walked in there and, hell, the woman put him to bed and took care of him, and months later, Jeep drove in when they started taking over France, and he got in there and left.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He relaxed until the troops arrived.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: That's what he did. He sat out the war. Yeah, he got a break.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Of course -- can I add something?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: They said, you know, some of the planes couldn't make it back, they ran out of fuel or something like that.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, that's another story.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: So, you know, they were over France or Germany.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No, they were over, when they went up to Kiel, Germany.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, Germany. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: The boat, not the boat, close to Sweden. We're out of gas, we don't have enough gas. Peeled off and landed in Sweden. Sat out the war. Some of them got shipped back unnoticed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, some of them they got back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that Sweden or Switzerland?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Sweden. Some went to Switzerland. Most of them went to Sweden. I guess it was closer, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because I think Switzerland, I think I had heard they would never let you, you had to stay there. They wouldn't let you leave if you were in Switzerland.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Sweden, they let some of them go.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Well, but they did get some back. My, you must have heard a lot of stories. I'm sorry, I'm interrupting.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Okay. I come back to the United States, I wish I'd stayed overseas, because, oh, the lamebrained people in charge, and I'll say the officers in charge, we come back by the thousands, didn't know what to do with us, wouldn't dare let us go, had no need for us. So, they gave us all basic training over again. Oh, we had some major got hit by the back, he turned his back to the group and he got conked out. Things like that. So, okay, after that happened, they shipped us all out to other bases.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was this basic training as if they were going to send you to the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: You got back in '44, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Still '44 when you got back?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, backtracking, do you have memories of your final mission?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Number 35?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You don't remember it.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No, I didn't do it. I mean, I did it, but, you know -- oh, I didn't finish yet. I got close to 35. Well, you're going to fly until we say you're done. So, I go to 35, they called me in, you're done. So, I did not have to sweat out the last mission, but that's how that happened. Then, after that, Texas, I forget where in Texas, all I remember is the drinking water was poison. Couldn't drink it. I got discharged from Wright Field Air Force base. I was out for five years, and then I got recalled to Korea.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: I joined the reserves. That was the biggest mistake of my life. I don't know if you want me to go into that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you go to Korea then?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: No. I lucked out again. Went there and went to Greenville Air Force base, South Carolina. What a farce, another farce. Oh, okay. Remember I says, I says the United States Air Corps, Army Air Corps. Okay, what I made a point of that was, now I was in the United States Air Force. Big difference. Went to Greenville, South Carolina, and it was trashed. I don't know how many months they used us guys, repair the barracks, build them up, put new lumber in, cut the grass, it was clear up to the windows. Unbelievable. We were laborers. We were all staff and tech and master sergeants, we're out there mowing grass and putting windows in and repairing this, repairing steps, repairing the roof, repairing. What a farce. Really a farce. Then, the only good part of that, it didn't have any civilian. (END OF TAPE ONE; BEGIN TAPE TWO.)

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: So they went into town and they bought turkeys and they bought chicken and they bought steaks. We ate well.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: But then you started flying.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, then we started flying. C119s. Cargo planes. The twin tails, I call them pregnant P38s. We did -- well, the pilots and the officers had to be trained in them, and us guys, we just maintained them, we had to maintain the ship now. We didn't have the ground crew do it for us, we maintained the ships, we had to gas them, we oiled them, we, we did everything, and so we, we were kind of home, the pilots had to shoot landings like mad, we shot landings all the time, and, and practiced in one, single engine approaches and all that. But, okay, well, I got news, well, we're going to Germany. I forget the name of the, one of the main airports in Ber -- in, yeah, Berlin. Well, okay, here we go again. And so we got close to pack up and gone, they called me in, you're through. So I went home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get out of the reserves after that?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, never went in again, I'll tell you that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm guessing you two didn't know each other when you were both in England?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Well, we knew each other but we didn't know each other.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: We went to the same high school at the same time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You just got together over there?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like in Great Britain between missions?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: It was pretty good. We could go to town. Of course, I was a little weird, I didn't drink. So, I went to town, went to the shows, and, that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Well, I took taxis back to town and forth. Even as a tech sergeant, I had the money to do that. Of course, four or five of us would get into a taxicab and come back. It wasn't that much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: That covers it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: He still likes the English movies.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah. I like, hey, I like the English. I don't care if they like me or not, I like the English. You could talk to them, and I knew a family over there, and they invited me in. Of course, they invited me in because they didn't have enough food for themselves. So, it was all right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They kind of adopted you?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, in a way, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get to spend a lot of time with them between missions and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, I would if I wanted to, as many, as much as I wanted to, welcome me with open arms, and they, of course, they gave me a cup of tea. Tea to burn, I guess. And they didn't drink it the way I did. Cream and sugar. So, in fact, one time I got a little late getting out of there and he lent me his bicycle and I rode the bicycle back to the base. I says, you got a lock? He says, what do you want a lock for? I said I want to give you your bike back in the morning.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Hoffman
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Earl Hoffman
sp.p: I think, I think that's it. I did enough, whether that's it or not, I think I did enough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think you got enough.
